text: Quick question.
Pick up your phone, open any feed, and scroll for ten seconds.
Now be honest: how much of that was actually made by a human?
Three years ago, the answer was easy.
All of it.
Today? Good luck.
Because somewhere in that feed there is a photo of a shrimp shaped like Jesus,
a news story about an event that never happened,
and a hit song by a band that does not exist.
The internet is filling up with garbage.
Cheap, fake, mass-produced garbage.
And the strange part is, nobody told it to.
Let's find out why.
This stuff actually has a name now.
We call it slop.
Slop.
Like the grey mush you pour into a pig trough.
And that is not an insult I invented.
"Slop" was literally named Word of the Year in 2025.
Now, one thing to get straight right away.
This is not a video about how AI is evil and the robots are coming.
That's a different video.
This is about something quieter, and honestly dumber.
The internet did not get worse because of some master plan.
It got worse because making fake content became almost free,
and the internet pays you for attention, not for quality.
So a flood started.
And it is still rising.
So what actually counts as slop?
Three things.
One: it looks fine for half a second.
Quick glance, looks normal.
Look closer, and it falls apart.
The hand has six fingers.
The words are gibberish.
A giant brand spends millions on a holiday ad and misspells its own name as "Coca-Coola."
That really happened.
Two: it costs the maker almost nothing, and it costs you everything.
Seconds to make.
But it eats your time, your attention, and your trust.
Three: it is made by the thousand.
Not one fake post.
Ten thousand fake posts, sprayed into the feed like a fire hose.
Looks fine, costs them nothing, made by the thousand.
That is slop.
A machine pretending to be a person, at full volume.
Now the important part.
Why does the flood keep coming?
Follow the money, slowly, because this is the whole video.
Step one.
Making content used to be expensive.
You needed a writer, a camera, a musician, time.
Now you need a prompt and ten seconds.
The cost dropped to almost zero.
Step two.
The platform does not pay you for being good.
It pays you for engagement,
and engagement just means clicks, likes, and time spent.
It rewards attention, not quality.
Step three.
So the smart move is not to make one great thing.
The smart move is to flood the zone:
post a thousand cheap things, and hope a few go viral.
Step four.
The algorithm that decides what you see?
It cannot really tell slop from real.
So it serves the slop anyway.
Step five.
The slop makes money, which pays for more slop.
The machine feeds itself.
That is the whole engine.
Cheap to make, paid by attention, impossible to filter.
Of course it floods.
And it is not just funny Facebook pictures anymore.
It got out.
Music.
A band called the Velvet Sundown passed one million listeners on Spotify
before people noticed that not a single member of the band was real.
Books.
People are selling AI mushroom-picking guides with fake photos.
Pick the wrong mushroom because a robot drew it,
and that one can actually kill you.
Kids.
One investigation found that around forty percent of the videos recommended to children looked like AI slop.
Forty out of every hundred:
nonsense cartoons with six-legged horses, all pretending to teach the alphabet.
Even your job.
There is now a word for the co-worker who sends you a beautiful AI document that says absolutely nothing.
You just got "workslopped."
On average, it costs the person who receives it about two hours to clean up.
So congratulations.
The slop is in your feed, your music, your kid's tablet, and your inbox.
Now let me be fair for a second, because this is where it gets interesting.
Not all AI content is slop.
A doctor using AI to explain a scan - not slop.
An artist using it as a tool - not slop.
Slop is about low effort and high volume.
It is not about the tool.
And no, this is not a secret plot.
There is a popular idea online called "dead internet theory,"
which says the government is secretly filling the web with bots to control your mind.
Relax. It's dumber than that.
Nobody is in charge.
No villain pressed a button.
The garbage spreads on its own, because the money rewards it.
And that is the uncomfortable part.
You cannot arrest an incentive.
So, why is the internet full of garbage now?
Not because AI is evil.
Not because of a conspiracy.
Because the internet is working exactly the way it was built to work.
It pays for attention.
Slop is very good at grabbing attention.
So slop wins.
Attention in. Garbage out.
The internet is not broken.
It is doing its job perfectly.
That is the problem.
But here is the small, useful upgrade.
Now you know the tells.
The six fingers.
The photo that is a little too perfect.
The story that is a little too good to be true.
You cannot stop the flood.
But you can stop being fooled by it.
And on an internet built on attention,
the person who pays attention on purpose is the one who wins.
We'll keep explaining the weird machine.
You keep your eyes open.
That's it for today.
